title: Probability Basics

steps.title: Probability is a fraction of outcomes
steps.content: When outcomes are equally likely, probability of an event = favourable outcomes ÷ total possible outcomes. It ranges from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain).
steps.example: A fair die has 6 outcomes. P(rolling an even number) = 3/6 = 1/2.

steps.title: A coin toss
steps.prompt: A fair coin is tossed once. What is the probability of getting heads?
steps.explanation: There are two equally likely outcomes, and one is heads. Probability = 1/2.
hints: A fair coin has two equally likely outcomes.
Only one of those outcomes is heads.

steps.title: Use the complement
steps.content: The probability that an event does not happen is 1 − P(event). This is useful when counting the opposite event is easier.
steps.example: Probability of at least one head in two tosses = 1 − P(no heads) = 1 − 1/4 = 3/4.

steps.title: Pick a card
steps.prompt: One card is drawn from a standard 52-card deck. What is the probability of drawing an ace?
hints: A standard deck has 52 cards in total.
There are four aces; simplify favourable outcomes divided by total outcomes.

steps.title: Independent events
steps.content: For independent events, multiply probabilities to get the probability that both happen. For mutually exclusive alternatives, add probabilities.
steps.example: Two fair coin tosses: P(two heads) = 1/2×1/2 = 1/4.

questions.prompt: A fair die is rolled. Probability of getting 5 is:
questions.explanation: One favourable result out of six equally likely results.

learning_objectives: Define a sample space and favourable event.
Calculate probability for equally likely outcomes.
Use complements to simplify 'at least one' questions.
Distinguish independent and mutually exclusive events.

common_misconceptions.misconception: A probability can be greater than 1.

common_misconceptions.correction: Independent events can occur together; independence means one event does not change the probability of the other.

common_misconceptions.misconception: Mutually exclusive and independent mean the same thing.
common_misconceptions.correction: Mutually exclusive events cannot occur together; non-zero independent events can occur together.

company_applications.practice: Count the sample space before selecting favourable outcomes.
Use a complement for 'at least one' problems.
Recognize when event probabilities should be multiplied.

srs_cards.question: How do independent events differ from mutually exclusive events?
srs_cards.answer: Independent events do not affect each other's probabilities; mutually exclusive events cannot happen at the same time.

quest.story: The academy wants to model uncertain events such as selecting a question or rolling a die. You must count outcomes carefully instead of guessing from intuition.
quest.mission: Build sample spaces, count favourable outcomes and use complements and independence.
